sb_prompt: DISCUSS GUN CONTROL.  WHERE DO YOU AND THE OTHER CALLER STAND ON A SCALE FROM 1 TO 10
turns: Hey, so I'm calling 'cause I'm an electrician and I've always thought guns should be easy to get, you know? What do you think? On a scale of one to ten, where are you?
I'm at a two, actually, because my cousin got shot by someone who bought a pistol right at the counter yesterday.

Oh man, that's really terrible, I'm sorry to hear that. But honestly, I don't get it; people just walk in and pick up a gun? My uncle works at a hardware store and he says the background checks are basically just a formality these days, so I guess that's why we need fewer laws.
Yeah, it's scary how easy it is sometimes, but honestly, I think the problem isn't the law, it's the people; my cousin was in trouble long before he ever walked into that store.
Yeah, but if the law is so easy to bypass, how do you stop someone who really doesn't want to hurt anyone from even thinking about getting one?
Exactly, that's the thing—my cousin was already struggling with anger and isolation for years; stopping him before he decides to buy a gun seems impossible just by closing a store door.
That makes sense, I guess, but it still feels like we're just ignoring a huge part of the puzzle when you think it's only the people.
I guess it's hard to regulate thoughts, so yeah, maybe the gun control part is just a band-aid on a wound that needs a doctor, not just a lock on the door.
So yeah, that's why I just think we should make the background check perfect or just ban them entirely, but I'm stuck because my whole life I've just assumed it was safer that way.

Look, I get where you're coming from, but if we just ban them, people will find other ways to get dangerous stuff, and honestly, talking to my cousin was the only thing that helped him feel like he wasn't alone.
Yeah, I get that people find other ways, but honestly, talking to him wouldn't have stopped him from getting a gun in the first place.
Yeah, but you have to admit, the easier it is to grab the gun, the less likely people are to think twice before they pull the trigger.

Yeah, I see what you're saying, but it still feels like the law is just a suggestion to me; if I walked into that store today with a bad day, I could probably walk out with a weapon before I even realized how much trouble I was in.
Exactly, you can walk out with the weapon before you realize it, and that's the scary part, but banning them doesn't fix the isolation that drove me to talk to my cousin in the first place.
I mean, but if you can't even get your hands on the tool that makes the threat real, does the isolation really matter as much?

I guess if the gun isn't there, you can't pull the trigger, so maybe the isolation matters less if there's literally nothing to grab, but then what are we banning them for if it doesn't solve the root cause?
I mean, if the isolation matters less without the means, maybe we should focus on fixing the isolation instead of the locks?
Exactly, but fixing people takes a long time and money, whereas a background check costs nothing and works right now.
Right, but I still feel like if the government just made it impossible to buy them, we'd stop the bad stuff before it even starts.
I guess you're right that banning it stops the means, but without the support that helps people like my cousin, you're just waiting for the next generation to figure it out on their own.
Yeah, but if we can't just lock the door, where do we put the sign that says "help is coming" when the money's not there?
I don't know, maybe we need both, or maybe we just need to stop waiting for the government to do the hard work.

So maybe you're right, we need both the locks and the counseling, but if the government isn't going to pay for the counseling, how do you expect regular people like me to know who to help before it's too late?
I mean, you can't just be the counselor for everyone, that's not really fair to you or the person in need.
I guess you're right, I just don't have the time or money to be that counselor, so the only thing I can do is lock the door.
Yeah, but I still think if the lock is strong enough, maybe you don't even need to be the counselor for everyone.
I guess locking the door buys us some time, but it still feels like we're just pushing the bad guys out to where someone else has to deal with them.
Yeah, maybe the lock keeps the gun off the street, but it doesn't stop the guy from getting mad in the first place.
Yeah, maybe locking the door is the only thing I can actually do, even if it doesn't fix the anger inside.
Yeah, maybe you're right, it's just a band-aid, but at least it might keep someone from hurting someone else right this second while we figure out the rest.
Yeah, you're probably right, if it buys us even a little time to actually help people, maybe that's something worth doing.
Yeah, that's the thing, it just keeps the bullet from flying right now while we figure out how to fix the rest.
Yeah, if it just keeps the bullet from flying for a few years, maybe that gives us enough time to actually build the support system you're talking about.
Yeah, exactly, if we just wait for the support system to get built, someone might pull the trigger today, so maybe the lock is worth buying just to keep the bullet in the holster for a little bit.
Yeah, maybe that's the only way we can actually save someone before the system catches up.
Yeah, I think that's probably all we can do right now.
Yeah, I guess that's fair, I just want to make sure the door is locked tight before we start looking for the master key.
Yeah, just locking the door tight is probably the only move we've got right now.
Yeah, I guess if locking the door is the only move we've got right now, then I'll stick to making sure the door is locked tight.
Yeah, I guess that's probably the best we can do.
